<reason>A close, high-quality debate. CON's mirrored Pokémon opening and "PRO regulates the flip, I regulate the money" line were the most memorable rhetoric, and the substitution argument was genuinely dangerous. But PRO answered it directly rather than dodging: the harm is the chase (decision under engineered uncertainty), fixed prices are "bounded by wanting," and removing the chance mechanic is the point of the motion. PRO's slot-token pressure question forced CON into a "sham vs real product" distinction that PRO then turned in closing (dust conversion exists to keep the child spinning; anti-avoidance says form doesn't decide category). Most decisively, CON conceded caps, forced odds, and killing one-tap — PRO's tools — and PRO showed the residual disagreement is only whether these rest on a self-declared birthdate (the failed honour system) or an enforcer with fines. CON's document-ID cost and Fortnite scarcity points were plausible but the latter arrived late in closing. PRO's repeated clipping (four turns) is a real execution cost that keeps the margin thin.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A3.1 slot-token question and its follow-through: CON answered that tokens are shams while duplicates convert to dust, and PRO's closing turned CON's own anti-avoidance principle against it, arguing dust conversion exists precisely to keep the loss from feeling final — undercutting CON's stake test.</best_rebuttal>
